A lot of “Black Monday” calls over the weekend. So far, $BTC is green and has bounced from around $80.5k to $83k.

The fears weren’t baseless. AI stocks had a rough week, oil was elevated, and the geopolitical headlines weren’t helping.

But today, oil has pulled back and US stock futures are higher. Trump’s waiver of the new Russia sanctions has also raised hopes of more fuel supply reaching the market.

That gives some context to the bounce. The problems haven’t disappeared, but markets have a little less pressure to deal with than the weekend headlines suggested.

My read: this looks more like a relief bounce than proof that everything is fine. US stocks haven’t even opened yet.

Still, there’s a difference between identifying real risks and confidently putting a date on a crash.

Being worried about the market is reasonable. Treating a red Monday as guaranteed is where the analysis gets lazy.

Think this is about the 3rd or 4th time just this year that people call for a "Black Monday".

As far as I know, those previous cases BTC front ran that by dumping during the weekend. Hence, making the case for a weak stock market on Monday more sense.

In this case not much is happening and I feel like it's just a lot of fear from the past few days of price action in especially the stock market.

If this year has shown us anything it is that markets really don't care about whatever is going on (to a certain extend).

Especially crypto has not been reacting to headlines and has been doing its own thing the past few months.

Correlation traders have been getting washed out during this time as well.

Over the months there have been just as many days that BTC was "correlated" to the Nasdaq 100 as days it was reversely correlated. So that says a lot.

Obviously if stocks crater deep then yes, BTC will see some weakness too. But I think these calls for "Black Monday" are super exaggerated. Keep in mind this definition was created in 1987 when the Dow dropped -22% in a single day.

People love naming previous big events to current situations and it never happens in the same way, especially when many call it beforehand.

I don't know what color Monday's candle will be but all the fear mongering going on just seems excessive at this point.

Just draw your high timeframe levels, sit back and relax. Don't overleverage (ever), have cash on the side and see how the market develops.

quote.text:
Jeff drank a bit too much of his own Kool-Aid in this recent Odd Lots clip. I think it's important to clear up a distinction that makes all the difference.

Democratizing access to wealth creation is NOT the same as democratizing access to speculation.

Many of us genuinely want broader participation in attractive investment opportunities. The growing wealth inequality produced by the current system is tearing at the seams of society, something I've spoken about many times.

But let's be clear: listing pre-IPO perpetual futures does absolutely nothing to democratize the wealth being created in private markets.

I've seen this misleading narrative pushed repeatedly by perp DEXs lately, and it needs to be called out.

A pre-IPO perp creates ZERO underlying wealth. It's a zero-sum contract before costs, and negative-sum after them. No capital flows to the company. No ownership changes hands. No new economic opportunity is created.

Every long has a short. There is no free lunch in simply going long something before its IPO, and funding costs can even determine the outcome more than any price moves. TRADING access is NOT INVESTING access.

In fact, in many ways pre-IPO perps are almost the antithesis of democratized access:

They create the illusion of participation in private-market wealth creation, while actually offering retail a speculative instrument whose mechanics they are often poorly equipped to understand.

The result is a playground for the FEW sophisticated traders who understand funding, oracle design, and liquidation mechanics to extract value from the MANY who don't.

To give credit where it's due, Robinhood's efforts toward sourcing actual employee shares, placing them into SPVs, and tokenizing genuine spot ownership are much closer to meaningful democratization.

That can unlock real economic value by allowing employees to exchange some of their expected upside for liquidity, while giving new investors actual economic exposure. A legitimate financial trade-off, without the funding-rate and liquidation shenanigans.

I'm strongly aligned with expanding access to investment opportunities. And I believe advances in AI and blockchain can dramatically lower the barriers to discovering, structuring, and distributing them.

But let's not BS ourselves that launching another zero-sum casino contract is moving the needle on wealth inequality.

What would actually move the needle is bringing real capital formation and ownership onchain. Giving investors access to productive, illiquid assets like data centers, GPUs, and select startup investing, where capital can actually finance growth and share in the resulting value creation.

These opportunities are harder to structure, underwrite, and bring to market, and we haven't seen many compelling implementations onchain yet. 

Hopefully this will change soon and, as the industry matures, we can direct more of our energy toward actually expanding access to wealth creation.

Clip below. Was glad to see @tracyalloway push back on this framing, and to Jeff's credit, after this he does seem to walk back his original position somewhat.

Think this is about the 3rd or 4th time just this year that people call for a "Black Monday".

As far as I know, those previous cases BTC front ran that by dumping during the weekend. Hence, making the case for a weak stock market on Monday more sense.

In this case not much is happening and I feel like it's just a lot of fear from the past few days of price action in especially the stock market.

If this year has shown us anything it is that markets really don't care about whatever is going on (to a certain extend).

Especially crypto has not been reacting to headlines and has been doing its own thing the past few months.

Correlation traders have been getting washed out during this time as well.

Over the months there have been just as many days that BTC was "correlated" to the Nasdaq 100 as days it was reversely correlated. So that says a lot.

Obviously if stocks crater deep then yes, BTC will see some weakness too. But I think these calls for "Black Monday" are super exaggerated. Keep in mind this definition was created in 1987 when the Dow dropped -22% in a single day.

People love naming previous big events to current situations and it never happens in the same way, especially when many call it beforehand.

I don't know what color Monday's candle will be but all the fear mongering going on just seems excessive at this point.

Just draw your high timeframe levels, sit back and relax. Don't overleverage (ever), have cash on the side and see how the market develops.

tweets.text:
One thing I’ve found interesting about exchange liquidity.

Volume doesn’t tell the whole story.

An exchange can have high volume without having great liquidity when you actually trade.

What matters is order book depth, active liquidity, and how much your order moves the price.

Trading costs are a good way to see this in practice.

For a $10K market order, we’re looking at the base tier taker fee plus half the effective spread.

That cost varies quite a bit across major venues. On perps, the gap is even bigger.

I also noticed on DeFiLlama that MEXC is now ranking #2 in active liquidity among all tracked exchanges, with $3.436B, behind only Binance at $4.065B.

A $10K trade on MEXC costs roughly half as much as on Binance or Bybit, for both spot and perps.

So volume is only one piece of the picture.

The more interesting question is how much usable liquidity is actually there when you need to trade, and what it costs to access it.

Patience until the daily close.

I looked into a lot of the coins CT has been hyping lately. These are my views after checking the actual fundamentals.

$NEAR: Intents show real usage, fee generation and buybacks. Volume is in the tens of billions cumulative with solid recent activity. Quantum-resistant signing is already optional on accounts with no migration needed. Buybacks are real, but issuance has often been higher so net supply is still expanding. Worth watching.

$ZEC: Privacy infrastructure is live and improving, with a growing shielded share of supply. Not a revenue play. More a bet on demand for financial privacy.

$TAO: Still one of the better decentralized AI setups. Subnets are generating real external revenue (recent estimates above $50M annualized) with actual customers and some revenue-funded buybacks. Emissions remain large relative to that, so I’m selective on what counts as genuine demand.

$ZRO: Strong cross-chain infrastructure with real usage. Stargate fees fund ZRO buybacks. Zero and ATLAS add an institutional settlement angle that is still mostly about what’s being built. Near-term unlock is a supply factor.

$STRK: Solid tech, real utility and growing BTCFi activity. Tokenomics remain a concern with roughly 127M STRK unlocking monthly through March 2027. Stronger demand would help absorb that supply.

$GRASS: One of the AI names actually reporting meaningful revenue. September third-party review showed about $14.5M in H1 2026. Interesting, though a material share of supply is still locked. Watching both adoption and dilution.

A few others:

$HYPE: One of the stronger business models in crypto. Real trading activity, substantial fees, and a clear mechanism sending a high share of those fees to HYPE purchases that get burned. Hard to ignore.

$MORPHO: Real adoption with genuine borrowing demand and major platform integrations. Product is finding traction, but direct token revenue capture is still limited.

$UNI: Fee switch improved the story. Established DEX usage now funds protocol-fee linked UNI burns. Better than the old governance-only setup, though burns have been modest so far.

I’m not dismissing projects just because CT is talking about them. Some have real revenue, some have good tech, and some still depend on what comes next.

There’s a difference between liking a project and paying any price for it. 
Good projects have turned into bad investments when expectations ran too far ahead of reality.

Being early to a good project and being early to a good trade are two different things.
